name: ACP-105

lead: ACP-105 is a selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) from the late 2000s. People take it hoping for more lean muscle and a leaner, harder look, with gentler androgenic effects than testosterone.

It works as a partial agonist at the androgen receptor, switching on muscle-building signalling more weakly than testosterone does. In castrated rats and mice it improved anabolic markers, and later animal work looked at cognitive decline and radiation-related deficits. No human trials have been published.

paras: Users describe it as an oral research chemical bought online and taken alongside resistance training, often during a lean-gain or recomposition phase. Reports of when changes show up vary, and no human protocol exists.

Human safety is unknown. SARMs as a class are banned in sport and have been linked in reports to liver injury and suppressed natural hormones. ACP-105 is unapproved and sold only as a research chemical.

angle.text: ACP-105 is a partial-agonist SARM that users take to add lean mass with milder androgenic effects. It partially activates the androgen receptor, which in castrated rats and mice improved anabolic markers and could translate to more muscle. Research so far is animal-only.

lead: ACP-105 is an investigational nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) with partial agonist activity relative to testosterone, described in a 2009 Journal of Medicinal Chemistry paper.[1][2] SARMs were designed to build muscle and bone while acting less on tissues such as the prostate, which is the reason bodybuilders and athletes show interest in them as a route to more muscle mass.[3]

It was discovered through a high-throughput screen using receptor selection and amplification technology, and improved anabolic parameters in castrated male rats.[1] Later animal work examined it in models of age-related cognitive decline and radiation-related deficits.[4][5]

It is not approved for any use. SARMs are banned in sport, and doping-control laboratories have published mass-spectrometric and metabolite studies of ACP-105 in human-sample and equine assays; a 2025 computational study estimated its toxicity profile.[6][7][8][9]

paras: ACP-105 was characterised in 2009 as a partial agonist of the androgen receptor, with the series discovered by screening in a receptor selection and amplification assay and tested for anabolic effect in castrated male rats.[1] Researchers have not settled how SARMs achieve tissue selectivity; proposals include lack of activation by 5-alpha-reductase in the prostate, differences in coregulator proteins between tissues, non-genomic signalling and differences in tissue uptake.[3]
Computational ADME and toxicity work published in 2025 described the compound's predicted absorption, distribution and toxicity, noting that its human safety profile has not been explored.[8][10]

ACP-105 is an aniline-type SARM structurally related to AC-262536 and RAD140 (vosilasarm).[2] Metabolites have been characterised in horse urine after oral administration, in vitro in equine liver preparations and in human in vivo samples, mainly to support doping control.[7][9][11]
The 2009 paper reported synthesis and structure-activity relationships of novel nonsteroidal SARMs and the characterisation of ACP-105 within that series.[1]

In a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, ACP-105 alone and in combination with an estrogen receptor beta agonist was reported to moderate cognitive deficits and amyloid-beta levels; alone it reduced anxiety-like behaviour, and with AC-186 it improved spatial memory.[2][4] A 2011 study examined its effects on rotarod performance and cued fear conditioning in sham-irradiated and irradiated female mice.[5]
No studies found in humans. All published efficacy work is in cells and animals.[1][4][5]

No human safety data were identified for ACP-105. Reviews of the SARM class describe elevated liver enzymes, reduced HDL cholesterol and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in some trials, case reports linking recreational SARM use to liver injury, and unknown cardiovascular risk. SARMs cannot be converted to estrogen, so estrogen-related effects are not expected.[3] The US FDA states that SARMs are unapproved and cannot legally be marketed as supplements or drugs; products sold as research chemicals are often reported to be mislabelled.[3]

SARMs have been prohibited in sport as anabolic agents under World Anti-Doping Agency rules since 2008, and metabolite identification for doping control was reported in 2014.[12][3] Papers describing mass-spectrometric characterisation of RAD140 and ACP-105 (2013) and equine metabolite studies (2021, 2022) were published to extend testing assays.[6][7][9][11]

SARMs are sold on gray markets, often labelled as research chemicals, and are used for muscle growth by bodybuilders and athletes; some jurisdictions treat marketing SARMs for human consumption as illegal, with criminal convictions reported.[3]
